subtopics.title: Visit Outcomes
subtopics.summary: Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing made a five-day official visit to India, his first since the political transition in Myanmar. The talks produced commitments on border security, a currency settlement framework, connectivity projects and scholarships. Both sides reaffirmed the Kaladan project and agreed to expedite the Trilateral Highway.
facts: Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing made a five-day official visit to India.
It was his first visit to India since the political transition in Myanmar.
Myanmar assured India that its territory would not be used by anti-India insurgent groups near the border.
Both sides agreed to promote greater use of the Rupee-Kyat settlement framework, operational since 2024.
Both countries reaffirmed their commitment to complete the Kaladan project at the earliest.
Efforts were announced to expedite the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway.
India increased the number of Mekong-Ganga ICCR scholarships for Myanmar students from 36 to 100.

subtopics.title: Historical Background
subtopics.summary: Much of India's North-East was under Burmese occupation until the Treaty of Yandaboo, signed in 1826 to end the Anglo-Burmese War of 1824-1826. The treaty established the current India-Myanmar boundary. General Sir Archibald Campbell signed it on behalf of the British.
facts: Much of India's North-East Region was under Burmese occupation until the Treaty of Yandaboo.
The Treaty of Yandaboo was signed in 1826.
The treaty ended the Anglo-Burmese War of 1824-1826.
General Sir Archibald Campbell signed the treaty on behalf of the British.
The treaty established the current India-Myanmar boundary.

subtopics.title: Strategic Importance and Relations
subtopics.summary: Myanmar is India's only ASEAN neighbour connected through both land and maritime boundaries, which makes it a geographic bridge to Southeast Asia. Cooperation with Myanmar is important for tackling insurgency, narcotics trafficking and cross-border crime. Ties are framed within India's Act East and Neighbourhood First policies.
facts: Myanmar is India's only ASEAN neighbour connected through both land and maritime boundaries.
India shares a border of 1643 km with Myanmar across Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram.
India and Myanmar share a maritime boundary in the Bay of Bengal.
Myanmar acts as a bridge between South Asia and South-East Asia.
India and Myanmar signed a Treaty of Friendship in 1951.
Cooperation with Myanmar is critical for tackling insurgency, narcotics trafficking, illegal arms smuggling and cross-border crime.
Myanmar is a member of BIMSTEC, a SAARC observer and part of the Mekong-Ganga Cooperation.
Bilateral trade is conducted under the ASEAN-India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA).

subtopics.title: Connectivity Projects
subtopics.summary: The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata with Sittwe Seaport in Rakhine, Myanmar, via the Bay of Bengal. The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway runs from Moreh in Manipur through Myanmar to Mae Sot in Thailand. Both projects featured in the outcomes of the visit.
facts: The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata with Sittwe Seaport in Rakhine, Myanmar.
The Kaladan project links India and Myanmar via the Bay of Bengal.
The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway is 1,360 km long.
The Trilateral Highway starts from Moreh in Manipur.
The Trilateral Highway passes through Myanmar before reaching Mae Sot in Thailand.
Both countries reaffirmed commitment to complete Kaladan at the earliest, and efforts to expedite the Trilateral Highway were announced.

subtopics.title: Myanmar's Political Background
subtopics.summary: The military seized power in Myanmar on February 1, 2021, after alleging huge irregularities in the November parliamentary polls. Aung San Suu Kyi and other civilian leaders were taken into custody, and a one-year state of emergency was declared. The NLD had won landslide victories in 2015 and 2020.
facts: The military seized power on February 1, 2021.
The military alleged huge irregularities in the November parliamentary polls.
The army declared a one-year state of emergency.
Myint Swe, a former general and the vice president, was to become acting president.
Aung San Suu Kyi and other civilian leaders were taken into custody hours before parliament was due to convene.
Internet and mobile phone communications were severely restricted and all banks were closed nationwide.

quizzes.passage: Myanmar's President, Min Aung Hlaing, undertook a five-day official visit to India, his first since the 2021 political transition in Myanmar. Myanmar holds a central place in India's Neighbourhood First Policy, its Act East Policy and its wider Indo-Pacific vision. It is the only ASEAN nation that shares a land border with India, and the two countries are connected by both land and sea. The booklet describes Myanmar as a geographic bridge linking India with Southeast Asia. To understand the relationship, it helps to look at the past. For a long period, a large part of the Indian territory lying in the east was under the control of the Myanmar side. This situation changed with a treaty known as the Treaty of Yandaboo. The treaty was signed by representatives of the British and of the Myanmar side. Its signing also brought an end to a war fought between the two powers. Myanmar's position also places it close to India's island territories, which makes maritime cooperation important for regional stability. The visit's outcomes included cooperation on counter-insurgency, as Myanmar assured India that its territory would not be used by anti-India insurgent groups operating near the frontier. Both countries also discussed connectivity in the wider relationship.

quizzes.passage: Myanmar has experienced a sharp change of control in recent years. The army took over the government after alleging huge irregularities in a parliamentary election held in November. Troops seized a city hall just ahead of the announcement, and the army then declared a state of emergency. Elected civilian leaders were taken into custody before the new parliament could convene. Communication services were restricted, and banks were closed across the country. A former general who was serving as vice president was set to become the acting head of state. The party that had secured two landslide victories in democratic elections was among those affected by these events. The booklet presents these events as what we know so far, and it lists them in a short timeline that starts with the allegations about the polls. The army's announcement was followed by a period of restricted communications and closed banks, as the timeline records. Several civilian politicians were held in the days that followed, according to the same account. Myanmar's current President has since made his first official visit to India after this change. The booklet describes that visit as a five-day official trip, and it notes that it was his first visit to India since the transition.

quizzes.passage: Myanmar's recent political history has been marked by a sudden change of control. The army moved against the elected government after alleging serious irregularities in a parliamentary election that had been held in November. Troops took over a key government building just ahead of the announcement, and the army then declared a state of emergency across the country. Elected civilian leaders were taken into custody hours before the new parliament was due to convene. The sitting President was among those detained. Communication services were restricted across the country, and all banks were closed nationwide. A former general who had served as vice president was positioned to take over as acting head of state. The booklet presents these events under the heading What we know so far, and the timeline it gives begins with the army's allegations and continues with the custody of leaders and the restrictions that followed. Myanmar's current President has since undertaken his first official visit to India since this transition, a five-day official trip. The booklet also notes the army's own account of why it acted, namely the alleged irregularities in the polls. Earlier elections had been won by the National League for Democracy, which secured landslide victories. The booklet's timeline therefore links the earlier electoral period with the takeover that followed.
